wrong: First-time property offenders
Profiling works best when an offender leaves repeated behavioral patterns, as in serial crimes.
Crimes with a confessed suspect
If the offender is already known, there is nothing left to profile.
Organized corporate fraud
Profiling reads behavior left at crime scenes, typical of serial violent crimes, not paper fraud.
Loop, Whorl, Accidental
Accidental is a type of whorl in the Henry system; the three main groups are loop, whorl and arch.
Radial, Ulnar, Tented
Radial and ulnar are kinds of loop, and tented is a kind of arch.
Plain, Central pocket, Double loop
These are types of whorl, not the three main patterns.
Visible print left in blood or ink
That is a patent print.
Molded print left in soft material
That is a plastic print.
Print taken on a card at booking
That is a recorded, or inked, print.
Invisible print that needs powder or chemicals
That is a latent print.
Three-dimensional impression in soft material like wax
That is a plastic print.
Partial print showing only part of the pattern
A partial print can be latent, patent or plastic; patent means a visible print made with a substance.
Print visible in blood
That is a patent print.
Hidden print needing powder
That is a latent print.
Print of only a fragment
That is a partial print; plastic means a molded 3D impression.
Black or dark powder
Dark powder does not contrast on dark surfaces; it is used on light ones.
Ninhydrin solution
Ninhydrin is a chemical for prints on paper, not a powder.
Silver nitrate solution
Silver nitrate is a chemical method for paper, not a powder.
Alphonse Bertillon
Bertillon devised anthropometry, identification by body measurements.
Sir Edward Henry
Henry developed the fingerprint classification system used in English-speaking countries.
Mathieu Orfila
Orfila is known as the Father of Toxicology.
flag: Hard question cr_017 says Sir Francis Galton is the Father of Fingerprint Identification, while this one says Juan Vucetich. Faculty should pick one source and fix the other. Galton was removed from this question's wrong options so it no longer marks him as wrong.

wrong: Blood only, from fresh stains
DNA can also come from saliva, hair roots and skin cells, not only blood.
Saliva and blood only
Hair with roots and skin cells also provide DNA.
Bone and teeth only
Bones and teeth do provide DNA, but so do blood, saliva, hair and skin cells.
Only blood and other body fluids
Hair roots, skin cells, bones and teeth also contain DNA.
Only cells taken from living persons
DNA is also recovered from the dead, including bones and teeth.
Only hair that was pulled out by the root
Hair roots are one source, but so are blood, saliva and skin cells.
Determining a person's ABO blood group
That is blood typing, which only places a person in a broad group.
Comparing ridge patterns on fingers
That is fingerprint identification (dactyloscopy).
Mapping every gene in a person's genome for research
That is genome sequencing; profiling compares a few highly variable markers to identify a person.
Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism
RFLP was the earlier method; STR analysis replaced it because it needs less DNA and is faster.
ABO and Rh blood group typing
Blood typing places a person in a broad class; it cannot identify an individual.
Mitochondrial DNA sequencing only
mtDNA is used for degraded samples or hair shafts, but routine profiling uses STRs.
Ultraviolet fluorescence examination
UV light shows erasures and some inks, but indented writing is best revealed by ESDA.
Thin-layer chromatography
TLC compares inks; it does not show indentations.
Infrared luminescence
Infrared shows altered or obliterated inks, not indentations.
Measure the caliber of the bullet
Caliber is measured with calipers or a micrometer.
Find powder residue
Gunshot residue is tested chemically or with an electron microscope, not with a comparison microscope.
Estimate the bullet's speed
Muzzle velocity is measured with a chronograph.
Study of the projectile's motion in the air
That is exterior ballistics.
Study of the projectile's effect on the target
That is terminal ballistics.
Study of wounds caused by projectiles in the body
That is wound ballistics, a branch of terminal ballistics.
Marks left by the firing pin
Firing pin marks are on the primer; rifling is the spiral grooves in the bore.
Narrowing at the shotgun muzzle
That is the choke of a shotgun.
Groove around a cartridge base
That is the extractor groove on the cartridge.
Marks left by the extractor and ejector
Those are marks on the cartridge case, not features of the barrel.
Raised ridges on the cartridge case
Lands and grooves are in the barrel, not on the cartridge.
Parts of a revolver cylinder
Lands and grooves are in the bore of a rifled barrel.
Measuring the weight and caliber of bullets
Weight and caliber are measured with a scale and calipers.
Detecting gunshot residue on a shooter's hands
Gunshot residue is tested chemically or with an electron microscope.
Estimating the distance of fire from wounds
Firing distance is estimated from powder patterns and test firing, not the comparison microscope.
Marks unique to one particular gun
Those are individual characteristics.
Random marks caused by gun wear
Wear produces individual characteristics, not class ones.
Serial number stamped on the frame
A serial number identifies one gun; it is not a class characteristic.
Overall length of the gun barrel
Barrel length is not caliber.
Weight of the bullet measured in grains
Bullet weight is stated in grains, separately from caliber.
Number of grooves inside the barrel
That is part of the rifling specifications, not caliber.
Study of projectile inside the gun
That is interior ballistics.
Study of impact on target
That is terminal ballistics.
Study of wound effects
That is wound ballistics.
Marquis color test
The Marquis test is for drugs like opiates and amphetamines.
Diphenylamine test
Diphenylamine detects nitrates from gunpowder residue.
Precipitin test
The precipitin test tells whether blood is human, after blood has been found.
Method of enlarging photos
That is photographic enlargement.
Method of measuring color
That is colorimetry or spectrophotometry.
Technique to develop prints
That is fingerprint development.
Enhancing faint photographs of evidence
That is photographic enhancement.
Matching bullets to the gun that fired them
That is firearms identification with a comparison microscope.
Comparing ridge details of latent prints
That is fingerprint comparison.
Blood stains invisible to the eye
Luminol or phenolphthalein is used to detect blood.
Gunshot residue on the hands
Diphenylamine or an electron microscope is used for gunshot residue.
Marijuana and other cannabis products
Cannabis is tested with the Duquenois-Levine test.
Cooling of the body after death
That is algor mortis.
Purplish skin from settled blood
That is livor mortis.
Breakdown of tissues by bacteria
That is decomposition (putrefaction).
The disease or injury that started the chain of events leading to death
That is the cause of death, for example a gunshot wound.
The physiological change by which the cause brings about death
That is the mechanism of death, for example hemorrhage.
The estimated time interval between death and the discovery of the body
That is the postmortem interval.

keep: All four are real forensic fields named the same way; the correct one is only slightly longer.
All four options use the same wording and are the same length.

wrong: Lawyer who handles medical malpractice cases
That is a lawyer; a medico-legal officer is a physician.
Police officer who guards the crime scene
Guarding the scene is a police task; a medico-legal officer is a physician.
Nurse who records injuries in the emergency room
Medico-legal examinations are done by a physician trained in legal medicine.
Stiffening of the muscles
That is rigor mortis.
Cooling of the body
That is algor mortis.
Greenish skin color from decay
That is the first sign of decomposition, usually on the abdomen.
Stiffening of muscles after death
That is rigor mortis.
Pooling of blood in the lowest parts
That is livor mortis.
Drying of the eyes and lips after death
That is postmortem drying (desiccation).
Identification by fingerprint patterns
That is dactyloscopy, which replaced the Bertillon system.
Identification by teeth
That is forensic odontology.
Identification by DNA markers
That is DNA profiling.
Sir Francis Galton
Galton studied fingerprints and showed they are unique and permanent.
Sir Edward Richard Henry
Henry developed a fingerprint classification system.
Juan Vucetich
Vucetich developed the fingerprint system used in Argentina.
System using body measurements and photographs
That is the Bertillon system.
System using dental records to identify persons
That is forensic odontology.
System of ten-print classification used in Argentina
That is Vucetich's system, used in Spanish-speaking countries.
Fingerprint patterns
That is dactyloscopy, which replaced the Bertillon system.
Ridge counts and patterns
That is the Henry system of fingerprint classification.
Blood types of suspects
Blood typing was not part of the Bertillon system.
Shows the whole scene from a distance
That is the overall or long-range shot.
Shows a single item filling the frame
That is the close-up.
Shows the scene from an aerial view
An aerial view is a kind of overall shot.
Provide images for news reports
Evidence photos are for the case record, not the media.
Replace the need to collect evidence
Photos document evidence; the items are still collected.
Identify suspects through facial recognition
Facial recognition is a separate identification technique.
Brain activity
A polygraph does not record brain waves.
Truthfulness directly
A polygraph records body responses; it does not measure truth itself.
Voice stress and pitch changes
That is voice stress analysis, a different device.
Brain waves, pupil size, and voice pitch
A polygraph does not record these.
Heart rate, body temperature, eye movement
Body temperature and eye movement are not polygraph channels.
Respiration, blood sugar, and muscle tone
Blood sugar and muscle tone are not measured by a polygraph.

keep: The correct answer is already the shortest option, and the wrong ones are the real polygraph channels.

wrong: Comparing handwriting to find the writer
That is handwriting identification by a document examiner, not graphology.
Analysis of inks to date a document
That is ink analysis.
Study of the history of writing systems and alphabets
That is paleography, the study of old writing.
Document in question
That is the questioned document.
Traced copy of a signature
That is a traced forgery.
Document with erasures
That shows alteration; an exemplar is a known standard.
Adding words between lines of a document
That is interlineation.
Copying a signature by tracing over it
That is a traced forgery.
Changing one figure or letter into another
That is alteration.
Writing of unknown authorship
That is the questioned writing.
Signature copied by freehand
That is a simulated forgery.
Torn or burnt document
A damaged document may be a questioned document, not a standard.
Genuine document with a faded signature
A faded signature does not make a genuine document false.
Certified true copy of an original
A certified copy is a lawful reproduction, not a forgery.
Duplicate original signed by all parties
A duplicate original is genuine.
Stamp placed on paper after printing
A stamp is applied on the surface; a watermark is formed in the paper itself.
Ink design printed on the paper surface
Printed designs sit on the surface of the paper.
Fibers that glow under ultraviolet light
Those are security fibers, not a watermark.
